## What is NeoBoard?

NeoBoard is an open-source dashboarding tool for hybrid database architectures. It connects to **Neo4j** and **PostgreSQL** databases, letting you build rich, interactive dashboards without writing frontend code.

**Key capabilities:**

- **12+ chart types** -- bar, line, pie, single value, table, graph visualization, map, JSON viewer, and more
- **Interactive parameters** -- dropdowns, date pickers, sliders, and text fields that filter data across all widgets
- **Form widgets** -- run write queries (INSERT, CREATE, UPDATE) directly from the dashboard
- **Multi-page dashboards** -- organize related views into pages with drag-and-drop layouts
- **Export and import** -- share dashboards as JSON files across NeoBoard instances
- **Role-based access** -- Admin, Creator, and Reader roles with granular write permissions
- **Encrypted credentials** -- AES-256-GCM encryption for all stored database passwords
- **Multi-tenancy** -- full tenant isolation for SaaS deployments

## Get Started

Choose the path that fits your setup:

| Method | Command | Time |
|--------|---------|------|
| **Docker (recommended)** | `neoboard demo` | ~5 minutes |
| **Local + Docker DBs** | `neoboard setup --mode local` | ~10 minutes |
| **Fully local** | `git clone` + `npm ci` + `npm run dev` | ~15 minutes |

See the [Installation guide](/getting-started/installation/) for full instructions.

Horizontal and vertical bar charts for comparing categories.

## Overview

The Bar Chart displays categorical data as rectangular bars whose lengths are proportional to the values they represent. Use it when comparing discrete categories or showing ranked data.

## Query Format

Return 2 or more columns: the first column is used as the category label (x-axis), and remaining columns become numeric series (y-axis). Multiple value columns produce grouped or stacked bars.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (m:Movie)
RETURN m.released AS label, count(*) AS value
ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 10
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT role AS label, COUNT(*) AS value
FROM "user"
GROUP BY role
ORDER BY value DESC
```

|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Orientation | select | vertical | Vertical bars (upward) or horizontal bars (left-to-right) |
| Stacked | boolean | false | Stack series on top of each other instead of side by side |
| Bar Width (px) | number | 0 (auto) | Width of each bar in pixels. 0 lets the chart auto-size |
| Bar Gap | text | 30% | Gap between bar groups as a percentage of bar width |
| Show Values | boolean | false | Display the numeric value as a label on each bar |
| Show Legend | boolean | true | Show the legend identifying each data series |
| X-Axis Label | text | (empty) | Custom label below the horizontal axis |
| Y-Axis Label | text | (empty) | Custom label beside the vertical axis |
| Show Grid Lines | boolean | true | Show faint horizontal reference lines |
| Axis Label Rotation | number | -1 (auto) | Override axis label angle (0-90). -1 auto-rotates at 8+ categories |
| Reference Lines | text | (empty) | JSON array of horizontal reference lines |
| Enable Scroll Zoom | boolean | false | Allow scroll-to-zoom on the data axis |
| Decimal Places | number | -1 (auto) | Fixed decimal places in tooltips (0-6) |

## Tips

- Use horizontal orientation when category labels are long -- it avoids overlapping text.
- Enable stacking when you want to show both the total and the contribution of each series.
- For large datasets, enable Scroll Zoom to let users explore a subset of categories interactively.
Input fields that execute write queries against your database.

## Overview

The Form widget renders a set of input fields that, when submitted, execute a write query (CREATE, MERGE, INSERT, UPDATE) against your database. Use it to build data entry forms, admin tools, or any workflow that requires writing data from the dashboard.

## Query Format

Write a mutation query with `$param_xxx` placeholders for each form field. The form fields editor (in the widget editor) lets you define the fields, their types, and validation rules.

### Cypher

```cypher
CREATE (n:Person {name: $param_name, email: $param_email, age: toInteger($param_age)})
```

### SQL

```sql
INSERT INTO people (name, email, age)
VALUES ($param_name, $param_email, $param_age)
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Submit Button Text | text | Submit | Label for the form submit button |
| Success Message | text | Form submitted successfully | Message shown after a successful submission |
| Reset on Success | boolean | true | Clear all form fields after a successful submission |

## Form Fields

Form fields are configured in the widget editor's **Fields** tab (not in Chart Options). Each field has:

- **Parameter name** -- maps to `$param_xxx` in the query
- **Label** -- display text shown to the user
- **Type** -- text, number, email, date, select, textarea, checkbox
- **Required** -- whether the field must be filled before submission
- **Default value** -- pre-filled value on form load

## Tips

- The connector must have `can_write` permission enabled by an admin for the form to execute. Additionally, each user who needs to submit forms must have **write permission** enabled on the Users page (toggle in the Write column). Both conditions are enforced server-side.
- Use descriptive parameter names like `$param_email` rather than `$param_1` to keep your query readable.
- Enable Reset on Success for data entry workflows where users submit multiple records in a row.
Interactive node-and-relationship visualization for Neo4j graph data.

## Overview

The Graph widget renders Neo4j nodes and relationships as an interactive force-directed graph. Users can drag nodes, zoom, and click to explore properties. This widget is only available for Neo4j connectors.

## Query Format

Return nodes, relationships, or paths -- not tabular data. The transform automatically extracts graph structures from the query result.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)
RETURN a, r, m
LIMIT 50
```

Paths also work:

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath((a:Person {name: 'Tom Hanks'})-[*]-(b:Person {name: 'Kevin Bacon'}))
RETURN p
```

### SQL

Graph visualization is not available for PostgreSQL connectors. Use a Neo4j connection for graph data.

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Layout | select | force | Node positioning algorithm: Force (physics simulation), Circular (ring), or Hierarchical (tree) |
| Node Size | select | medium | Visual size of each node: Small, Medium, or Large |
| Show Labels | boolean | true | Show the node label (first string property) on each node |
| Show Relationship Labels | boolean | true | Show the relationship type name on each edge |
| Enable Physics | boolean | true | Enable physics simulation so nodes repel and edges act as springs |

## Tips

- Add a `LIMIT` to your query to keep the graph readable -- more than 200 nodes can get cluttered.
- Use the Hierarchical layout for tree-like data (org charts, category hierarchies).
- Disable physics after the layout stabilizes if you want to manually position nodes by dragging them.
Embed an external web page within a dashboard widget.

## Overview

The iFrame widget embeds an external web page directly into a dashboard. Use it to include third-party tools, documentation pages, or external dashboards alongside your NeoBoard widgets. No query or database connection is required.

## Query Format

This widget does not use a query. Configure the URL and settings in the Chart Options panel.

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| URL | text | (empty) | The URL of the external page to embed. Must be an https:// URL |
| Title | text | Embedded content | Accessible title for screen readers |
| Sandbox Policy | text | (empty) | HTML sandbox attributes controlling what the embedded page can do |

## Sandbox Policy

The sandbox field accepts standard HTML `sandbox` attribute values. Common values:

| Value | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| (empty) | Maximum restrictions: no scripts, no forms, no popups |
| `allow-scripts` | Allow JavaScript execution |
| `allow-forms` | Allow form submission |
| `allow-same-origin` | Treat embedded content as same-origin |
| `allow-scripts allow-same-origin` | Allow scripts and same-origin access (use with trusted content only) |

## Tips

- Always use `https://` URLs. Most browsers block mixed content (HTTP inside HTTPS).
- Leave the Sandbox Policy empty for untrusted content to apply maximum restrictions.
- Some sites block embedding via `X-Frame-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy` headers -- if the page appears blank, the target site may not allow iframing.
Overview of all widget and chart types available in NeoBoard.

NeoBoard includes a variety of chart and widget types to visualize data from Neo4j and PostgreSQL. Each type expects a specific query result shape and offers its own configuration options.

## Available Chart Types

| Type | Description | Data Sources |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| [Bar Chart](/charts/bar) | Vertical or horizontal bars for comparing categories | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Line Chart](/charts/line) | Trend lines and time series | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Pie / Doughnut](/charts/pie) | Proportional slices for part-to-whole comparisons | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Single Value](/charts/single-value) | One large number (KPI card) with optional trend | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Data Table](/charts/table) | Sortable, filterable, paginated data grid | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Graph](/charts/graph) | Interactive node-and-relationship visualization | Neo4j only |
| [Map](/charts/map) | Geographic markers on a Leaflet map | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [JSON Viewer](/charts/json) | Collapsible JSON tree for raw data inspection | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Form](/charts/form) | Input fields that execute write queries | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |
| [Markdown](/charts/markdown) | Static rich text content (no query needed) | N/A |
| [iFrame](/charts/iframe) | Embed an external web page | N/A |
| [Parameter Select](/charts/param-select) | Dropdown, date picker, or other input that feeds parameters to other widgets | Neo4j, PostgreSQL |

## Choosing a Chart Type

- **Comparing categories?** Use a [Bar Chart](/charts/bar).
- **Showing trends over time?** Use a [Line Chart](/charts/line).
- **Part-to-whole breakdown?** Use a [Pie Chart](/charts/pie).
- **Single KPI metric?** Use a [Single Value](/charts/single-value).
- **Exploring raw data?** Use a [Data Table](/charts/table) or [JSON Viewer](/charts/json).
- **Visualizing a graph?** Use the [Graph](/charts/graph) widget (Neo4j only).
- **Geographic data?** Use the [Map](/charts/map) widget.
- **Collecting user input?** Use a [Form](/charts/form) or [Parameter Select](/charts/param-select).

## Shared Options

Most chart types share these common options:

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Show Refresh Button | Adds a manual refresh button to the widget header |
| Manual Run | Requires the user to click "Run Query" before executing |
| Cache Mode | TTL (time-based refresh) or Forever (cache until manual refresh) |
| Color Palette | Color scheme for chart series (ECharts-based charts only) |
| Colorblind Mode | Overlays patterns so series are distinguishable without color (ECharts-based charts only) |
Collapsible JSON tree for inspecting raw query results.

## Overview

The JSON Viewer renders query results as an interactive, collapsible JSON tree. Use it for debugging queries, inspecting nested data structures, or displaying complex objects that do not fit neatly into charts or tables.

## Query Format

Return any data -- all query results are rendered as a JSON tree. Particularly useful for queries that return nested or complex objects.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
RETURN properties(n) AS data
LIMIT 5
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT row_to_json(u) AS data
FROM users u
LIMIT 5
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Initial Expand Depth | number | 2 | How many levels deep the tree is expanded on first render (0 = fully collapsed) |
| Font Size | select | sm | Font size for the JSON syntax highlighting: Small, Medium, or Large |
| Show Copy Button | boolean | true | Show a button to copy the full JSON payload to the clipboard |
| Theme | select | dark | Color theme for syntax highlighting: Dark or Light |

## Tips

- Set Initial Expand Depth to 0 for large payloads so users can selectively expand the sections they need.
- Use the Copy Button to quickly grab query results for use in other tools or for sharing.
- The JSON Viewer is a great debugging tool during dashboard development -- switch to a proper chart type once your query is finalized.
Trend lines and time series for tracking changes over time.

## Overview

The Line Chart connects data points with lines, making it ideal for showing trends, time series, and continuous data. Multiple series are rendered as separate lines for comparison.

## Query Format

Return 2 or more columns: the first column is used as the x-axis (dates, numbers, or labels), and remaining columns become numeric series.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (m:Movie)
RETURN m.released AS year, count(*) AS movies
ORDER BY year
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at)::date AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS signups
FROM "user"
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Smooth Curve | boolean | false | Render lines as smooth curves instead of straight segments |
| Fill Area | boolean | false | Fill the area beneath the line to emphasise volume |
| Line Width (px) | number | 2 | Stroke width of the line in pixels |
| Stepped Line | boolean | false | Draw the line as a step function for discrete state changes |
| Show Data Points | boolean | false | Draw a dot at each data point along the line |
| Show Grid Lines | boolean | true | Show faint horizontal reference lines |
| X-Axis Label | text | (empty) | Custom label below the horizontal axis |
| Y-Axis Label | text | (empty) | Custom label beside the vertical axis |
| Show Legend | boolean | true | Show the legend identifying each data series |
| Reference Lines | text | (empty) | JSON array of horizontal reference lines |
| Sampling Threshold | number | 1000 | Enable LTTB downsampling when points exceed this count. 0 disables |
| Sampling Method | select | lttb | Algorithm for downsampling: LTTB, Average, Max, or Min |
| Enable Scroll Zoom | boolean | false | Allow scroll-to-zoom on the data axis |
| Decimal Places | number | -1 (auto) | Fixed decimal places in tooltips (0-6) |

## Tips

- Enable Fill Area and Smooth Curve together for a polished area chart look.
- For datasets with more than 1,000 points, the LTTB sampling algorithm keeps the chart responsive while preserving visual shape.
- Use Stepped Line for data that changes in discrete jumps (e.g., pricing tiers, status codes).
Geographic markers on a Leaflet map for location-based data.

## Overview

The Map widget plots geographic data points as markers on an interactive Leaflet map. Use it for location-based data such as store locations, events, or any dataset with latitude and longitude columns.

## Query Format

Return columns containing latitude and longitude values. Column names must contain "lat" and "lng" (or "lon"/"long"). An optional label column (matching "name", "label", or "title") is shown in marker popups.

### Cypher

> The demo Neo4j dataset does not include geographic data. The example below assumes you have loaded nodes with latitude/longitude properties.

```cypher
MATCH (s:Location)
RETURN s.latitude AS lat, s.longitude AS lng, s.name AS name
```

### SQL

> The demo PostgreSQL database does not include geographic data. Replace the table and column names with your own.

```sql
SELECT latitude AS lat, longitude AS lng, name
FROM locations
WHERE latitude IS NOT NULL
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Tile Layer | select | osm | Base-map provider: OpenStreetMap, Carto Light, or Carto Dark |
| Default Zoom | number | 3 | Initial zoom level (1 = world, 18 = street level) |
| Min Zoom | number | 2 | Minimum zoom level the user can zoom out to |
| Max Zoom | number | 18 | Maximum zoom level the user can zoom in to |
| Auto-fit Bounds | boolean | true | Automatically pan and zoom to fit all markers on load |
| Marker Size (px) | number | 6 | Radius of each marker circle in pixels |
| Cluster Markers | boolean | false | Group nearby markers into cluster badges at lower zoom levels |
| Show Popup on Click | boolean | true | Show a popup with row data when clicking a marker |

## Tips

- Enable Cluster Markers when plotting hundreds of points to keep the map readable at low zoom levels.
- Use Carto Dark or Carto Light tile layers for a cleaner background when the data overlay is the focus.
- Set Auto-fit Bounds to true so the map automatically frames all your data points on first load.
Static rich text content for dashboard annotations and instructions.

## Overview

The Markdown widget renders static rich text content directly on the dashboard. Use it for headings, instructions, documentation links, or any explanatory text that helps users understand the dashboard. No query or database connection is required.

## Query Format

This widget does not use a query. Content is entered directly in the Chart Options panel.

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Markdown Content | text | (empty) | Markdown text to render. Supports headings, bold, italic, links, lists, code blocks, and blockquotes |

## Supported Markdown Syntax

```markdown
# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3

**Bold text** and *italic text*

- Bullet list item
- Another item

1. Numbered list
2. Second item

[Link text](https://example.com)

> Blockquote

`inline code` and code blocks with triple backticks
```

## Tips

- Use Markdown widgets as section headers to organize a dashboard into logical groups.
- Add a brief description at the top of a dashboard explaining what data sources it covers and how to interpret the charts.
- Markdown widgets resize with the grid layout, so keep content concise to avoid scrolling in small widgets.
Dropdown, date picker, and other input controls that feed parameters to other widgets.

## Overview

Parameter Select widgets collect user input and pass it to other widgets' queries as `$param_name` variables. They enable interactive filtering across an entire dashboard without modifying queries. Parameter widgets do not display data themselves.

## Parameter Types

| Type | Input Control | Value Produced |
|------|--------------|----------------|
| Select | Dropdown (populated by a seed query) | Single string |
| Text | Free-text input | String |
| Number | Numeric input | Number |
| Date | Date picker | ISO date string |
| Date Range | Start/end date pickers | `{start, end}` object |
| Boolean | Toggle switch | `true` or `false` |
| Multiselect | Multi-value dropdown | Array of strings |
| Slider | Range slider | Number |

## Seed Query (Select / Multiselect)

For Select and Multiselect types, a seed query populates the dropdown options. Return a single column -- each row becomes an option.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (m:Movie)
RETURN DISTINCT m.released AS year
ORDER BY year
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT role FROM "user" ORDER BY role
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Placeholder | text | (empty) | Hint text shown when no value has been chosen |
| Search-as-you-type | boolean | true | Allow typing to filter the option list in real time |
| Default Value | text | (empty) | Value used on dashboard load when no selection has been made |
| Sync to URL | boolean | false | Persist the selected value as a URL parameter for sharing and page reloads |

## Using Parameters in Queries

Other widgets reference parameter values using `$param_name` syntax in their queries:

```cypher
MATCH (m:Movie)
WHERE m.released = $param_year
RETURN m.title, m.released
ORDER BY m.title
```

```sql
SELECT name, email FROM "user"
WHERE role = $param_role
ORDER BY name
```

## Tips

- Enable Sync to URL so users can bookmark or share a dashboard with specific filter values pre-selected.
- Set a Default Value for parameters that should always have a selection on first load.
- See [Parameters](/dashboards/parameters) for details on parameter substitution, cascading parameters, and advanced usage.

## Overview

The Pie Chart shows how a total is divided among categories. Each slice represents a category's share of the whole. Enable donut mode to add a center cutout, which is useful for displaying a total or label in the middle.

## Query Format

Return exactly 2 columns: the first column is the slice label (string), and the second column is the numeric value.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[r]->(m:Movie)
RETURN type(r) AS category, count(*) AS total
ORDER BY total DESC
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT role AS category, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM "user"
GROUP BY role
ORDER BY total DESC
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Donut Style | boolean | false | Cut a hole in the centre to render as a donut |
| Rose/Nightingale Mode | boolean | false | Vary each slice's radius by its value |
| Label Position | select | outside | Where to place slice labels: outside, inside, or center |
| Show Labels | boolean | true | Show the category name on each slice |
| Show Percentage | boolean | true | Show the percentage value on each slice |
| Show Legend | boolean | true | Show the legend identifying each slice |
| Sort Slices by Value | boolean | false | Sort slices largest-first for a cleaner layout |
| Top N Slices | number | 0 (all) | Show only the top N slices; group the rest into "Other" |
| Donut Center Text | text | (empty) | Custom text in the donut center. Blank shows the total |
| Decimal Places | number | -1 (auto) | Fixed decimal places in tooltips (0-6) |

## Tips

- Use Top N Slices to avoid visual clutter when you have many small categories -- the rest are grouped into "Other".
- Enable Donut Style and set Donut Center Text to display a KPI in the middle of the chart.
- Rose/Nightingale mode works well when you want to emphasize the magnitude difference between categories.
Large KPI card for displaying one key metric.

## Overview

The Single Value widget displays a single number prominently, making it ideal for KPIs and key metrics. It supports prefixes, suffixes, number formatting, and an optional trend indicator comparing to a previous period.

## Query Format

Return a single row with 1 numeric column. For trend mode, return 2 rows where the first row is the current period and the second row is the previous period.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN count(p) AS total
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM "user"
```

For trend mode (2 rows):

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM "user" WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'
UNION ALL
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM "user" WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '14 days'
  AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'
ORDER BY total DESC
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Title | text | (empty) | Custom heading shown above the value |
| Prefix | text | (empty) | Text prepended to the value (e.g., "$", "EUR") |
| Suffix | text | (empty) | Text appended to the value (e.g., "%", " items") |
| Decimal Places | number | -1 (auto) | Fixed decimal places (0-6). -1 for automatic |
| Font Size | select | lg | Size of the displayed value: Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large |
| Number Format | select | plain | Plain, Comma (1,234), Compact (1.2k), or Percent |
| Show Trend Indicator | boolean | false | Show a trend arrow comparing current to previous period (requires 2 rows) |

## Tips

- Combine Prefix and Number Format for currency displays: set Prefix to "$" and Number Format to "Comma" for values like "$1,234,567".
- Enable Show Trend Indicator and return two rows to add an up/down arrow showing period-over-period change.
- Use Compact number format for large numbers that would otherwise be hard to read at a glance.
Sortable, filterable, paginated data grid for tabular results.

## Overview

The Data Table displays query results as a fully interactive grid with sorting, filtering, pagination, and optional row grouping. Use it when you need to browse raw data or let users explore results interactively.

## Query Format

Return any columns -- all are displayed as-is in the table. Column names become the header labels.

### Cypher

```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)
RETURN p.name AS actor, m.title AS movie, m.released AS year
ORDER BY m.released DESC LIMIT 100
```

### SQL

```sql
SELECT name, email, created_at, role
FROM "user"
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| Enable Sorting | boolean | true | Allow clicking column headers to sort rows |
| Row Selection | boolean | false | Allow selecting individual rows by clicking |
| Global Search | boolean | true | Show a search box that filters across all columns |
| Column Filters | boolean | true | Show per-column filter inputs below each header |
| Column Resizing | boolean | false | Allow drag-to-resize column borders |
| Enable Pagination | boolean | true | Show Previous/Next controls for paging |
| Page Size | number | 10 | Number of rows shown per page |
| Empty Message | text | No results | Text displayed when the query returns no rows |
| Enable Row Grouping | boolean | false | Allow grouping rows by column values |
| Group By Columns | column-multi-select | (none) | Columns to group by. Order determines nesting hierarchy |
| Aggregation Function | select | sum | Aggregation for numeric columns in groups: Sum, Average, Median, Count, Min, Max |

## Tips

- Combine Global Search with Column Filters for power users who need to drill into specific column values.
- Enable Row Grouping with an aggregation function to create summary views without changing your query.
- Set Page Size to match your widget height -- 10-15 rows is typical for a half-height widget.

Complete reference for all NeoBoard CLI commands.

All commands are run from the repository root as `node cli/dist/index.js <command>`. If you have the CLI installed globally, replace with `neoboard <command>`.

## setup

Full setup in one command: runs `init`, then `start` (which includes migrations).

```bash
neoboard setup [--mode <docker|local>]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `--mode <mode>` | `docker` | `docker` -- everything in containers. `local` -- app locally, databases separate. |

```bash
# Docker setup (default)
neoboard setup

# Local setup
neoboard setup --mode local
```

## init

Initialize project configuration and install dependencies. Creates `neoboard.config.json` and `.neoboard.local`. In local mode, also installs npm dependencies and generates `app/.env.local`.

```bash
neoboard init [--mode <docker|local>]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `--mode <mode>` | `docker` | `docker` or `local`. |

```bash
neoboard init --mode local
```

## start

Start NeoBoard services and run database migrations. In Docker mode, launches containers via `docker compose`. In local mode, connects to your running PostgreSQL and Neo4j instances.

```bash
neoboard start
```

No options. The mode is read from `.neoboard.local` (set during `init` or `setup`).

```bash
neoboard start
```

## stop

Stop Docker containers. Only applies to Docker mode.

```bash
neoboard stop [--volumes]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `--volumes` | `false` | Also remove data volumes, giving you a clean slate. |

```bash
# Stop but keep data
neoboard stop

# Stop and delete all data
neoboard stop --volumes
```

## dev

Start the Next.js dev server with hot reload. Only works in local mode. If databases are not running, attempts to start them via Docker Compose automatically.

```bash
neoboard dev
```

No options. Validates that `app/.env.local` has all required variables before starting. Press `Ctrl+C` to stop.

```bash
neoboard dev
```

## status

Show the health of PostgreSQL, Neo4j, and the NeoBoard app. Displays mode, version, container count, and migration status.

```bash
neoboard status
```

```bash
neoboard status
# Mode:        docker
# Version:     1.0.0
# Docker:      running (3 containers)
#
# Service      Status
# ---
# PostgreSQL   healthy (localhost:5432)
# Neo4j        healthy (localhost:7687)
# App          healthy (http://localhost:3000)
#
# Migrations:  12 applied (latest: 0012_add_sharing)
```

## doctor

Check that all prerequisites are met: Docker daemon, Docker Compose v2, Node.js version, port availability, `node_modules`, and `.env.local`. Exits with code 1 if any check fails in Docker mode. In local mode, Docker checks are downgraded to warnings.

```bash
neoboard doctor
```

```bash
neoboard doctor
```

## demo

Set up a full demo environment with sample data. Runs `setup`, then seeds Neo4j with graph data and PostgreSQL with a demo user and sample dashboards.

```bash
neoboard demo [--mode <docker|local>]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|

NeoBoard is configured through environment variables and an optional config file. Create a `.env.local` file in the `app/` directory (i.e. `app/.env.local`).

## Example `.env.local`

```bash

MAX_QUERY_ROWS=1000
QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000
```

Generate secrets with:

```bash
# NEXTAUTH_SECRET
openssl rand -base64 32

# ENCRYPTION_KEY
openssl rand -hex 32
```

## Required Variables

| Variable | Description | Example |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| `DATABASE_URL` | PostgreSQL connection string for metadata | `postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/neoboard` |
| `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` | Secret for signing session tokens | Output of `openssl rand -base64 32` |
| `ENCRYPTION_KEY` | AES-256 key for encrypting stored credentials | Output of `openssl rand -hex 32` |

## Optional Variables

| Variable | Description | Default |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| `NEXTAUTH_URL` | Public URL of the NeoBoard instance | `http://localhost:3000` |
| `DEFAULT_TENANT_ID` | Default tenant for single-tenant deployments | `default` |
| `MAX_QUERY_ROWS` | Maximum rows returned per query | `1000` |
| `QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS` | Default query timeout in milliseconds | `30000` |

## SSO / OIDC Variables

SSO requires `NEOBOARD_EDITION=enterprise`. Set the three required OIDC variables plus the edition flag to enable single sign-on. See the [SSO guide](/authentication/sso) for full setup instructions and IdP examples.

| Variable | Description | Default |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| `OIDC_ISSUER` | OIDC issuer URL | (required for SSO) |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | OIDC client identifier | (required for SSO) |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | OIDC client secret | (required for SSO) |
| `OIDC_DISPLAY_NAME` | Login button label | `SSO` |
| `OIDC_CLAIM_KEY` | IdP claim for role mapping | (unset — no mapping) |
| `OIDC_DEFAULT_ROLE` | Role when no claim matches | `creator` |
| `OIDC_ENFORCE_SSO` | Hide password form for non-admins | `false` |

## Enterprise Variables

Set `NEOBOARD_EDITION=enterprise` to enable enterprise features like the Admin UI for multi-provider SSO, custom roles, and more.

| Variable | Description | Default |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| `NEOBOARD_EDITION` | Set to `enterprise` to enable enterprise features | (unset — community edition) |

You can also use a `neoboard.config.json` file in the project root for non-secret settings:

TypeScript conventions, lint rules, and coding standards.

## TypeScript

- **Strict mode** enabled across all packages
- No `any` without a comment explaining why
- Prefer `unknown` over `any` for untyped values
- Use explicit return types for exported functions

## Linting

```bash
npm run lint                    # Lint all packages
cd app && npx next lint --fix   # Auto-fix app/ lint errors
```

Run lint after every change to `app/`.

## Naming Conventions

| Item | Convention | Example |
|------|-----------|---------|
| Files | kebab-case | `chart-registry.ts` |
| Components | PascalCase | `BaseChart` |
| Functions | camelCase | `buildExportPayload` |
| Constants | UPPER_SNAKE | `MAX_QUERY_ROWS` |
| Types/Interfaces | PascalCase | `ConnectionCredentials` |
| Test files | `*.test.ts` | `chart-registry.test.ts` |

## Package Boundaries

These are **strict** — violations will be caught in code review:

- `component/` — NO API calls, NO stores, NO imports from `app/`
- `connection/` — NO UI, NO React, NO imports from `app/` or `component/`
- `app/` — CAN import from `component/` and `connection/`

## Query Safety

- **Always** use parameterized queries
- **Never** interpolate user input into query strings
- **Never** modify or wrap user queries
- Enforce read-only at the driver/transaction level

NeoBoard follows a strict **Test-Driven Development** (TDD) workflow.

## TDD Workflow (Mandatory)

1. **Red** — Write a failing test describing expected behavior
2. **Green** — Write the minimum code to make it pass
3. **Refactor** — Clean up without breaking tests

Every new behavior, bug fix, and edge case gets a test. No exceptions.

## Test Boundaries

| Layer | Tool | Package | Examples |
|-------|------|---------|---------|
| Pure functions | Vitest | `app/` | chart-registry, date-utils, query-hash |
| API routes | Vitest (mocked DB/auth) | `app/` | Validation, permissions, error handling |
| Zustand stores | Vitest (no mocks) | `app/` | State transitions, cascading logic |
| UI components | Vitest + RTL | `component/` | Isolated rendering, props |
| Integration | Jest + Testcontainers | `connection/` | Real DB queries |
| Full flows | Playwright | `app/` | Real rendering, real data |

**Important**: Do NOT add `@testing-library/react` render tests in `app/`. UI rendering is tested via Playwright E2E. Vitest in `app/` is for pure logic only.

## Coverage Target

**80% per package** (unit + E2E combined).

Track coverage with:
```bash
cd app && npm run test:coverage
cd component && npm run test:coverage
cd connection && npm run test:coverage
```

## Test File Location

Tests live in `__tests__/` directories next to the file under test:

```
src/lib/
├── chart-registry.ts
├── __tests__/
│   └── chart-registry.test.ts
```

## Common Patterns

### Mocking API Routes

```typescript
const mockDb = { select: vi.fn(), insert: vi.fn() };
vi.mock("@/lib/db", () => ({ db: mockDb }));
vi.mock("@/lib/auth/session", () => ({ requireSession: mockRequireSession }));
vi.mock("next/server", () => nextResponseMockFactory());
```

### E2E Test Fixtures

```typescript
import { test, expect } from "./fixtures";

test("create dashboard", async ({ page, authPage }) => {
  await authPage.login({ email: "alice@example.com", password: "password123" });
  // ...
});
```

Step-by-step guide to implementing a new parameter type.

This guide covers adding a new interactive parameter type to NeoBoard.

## Overview

A parameter type requires:
1. Add to the `ParameterType` union
2. Handle in the parameter store
3. Create the widget component
4. Add formatting logic
5. Wire into the renderer

## Step 1: Define the Type

Add your type to the parameter type union:

```typescript
export type ParameterType =
  | "select"
  | "text"
  | "number"
  | "date"
  | "dateRange"
  | "boolean"
  | "multiselect"
  | "slider"
  | "your-type"; // Add here
```

## Step 2: Update Parameter Store

In `app/src/stores/parameter-store.ts`, handle your type's default value and coercion:

```typescript
case "your-type":
  return coerceYourType(rawValue);
```

The store manages parameter state, persistence, and cross-widget dependencies.

## Step 3: Create Widget Component

In `component/src/components/composed/parameter-widgets/`:

```typescript
export function YourTypeWidget({
  value,
  onChange,
  label,
  ...props
}: YourTypeWidgetProps) {
  return (
    // Your input UI
  );
}
```

**Boundary rule**: The component must be pure UI — no API calls, no stores.

## Step 4: Add Formatting

In `app/src/lib/format-parameter-value.ts`, add formatting for query substitution:

```typescript
case "your-type":
  return formatYourType(value);
```

## Step 5: Wire into Renderer

Update `app/src/components/parameter-widget-renderer.tsx` to render your widget type.

## Step 6: Write Tests

1. **Store test** — verify coercion and state management
2. **Component test** — render with mock props (in `component/`)
3. **E2E test** — add parameter widget to a dashboard and verify it filters data

Configure OIDC single sign-on providers to enable SSO login for your organization.

import { Aside, Steps, Tabs, TabItem } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

NeoBoard supports OIDC-based single sign-on (SSO). Users can sign in with their organization's identity provider (Okta, Azure AD/Entra, Google Workspace, Keycloak, Auth0, etc.) instead of managing separate NeoBoard passwords.

## How It Works

1. SSO is configured via **environment variables** (recommended) or the **Admin UI**
2. The login page shows "Sign in with [Provider]" buttons above the password form
3. Clicking a button redirects the user to the identity provider (IdP)
4. After authentication, the IdP redirects back to NeoBoard with an authorization code
5. NeoBoard exchanges the code for tokens, reads the user's profile and group claims, and creates or links the user account

## Prerequisites

Before configuring SSO, you need:

- `NEOBOARD_EDITION=enterprise` set in your environment
- An OIDC client registered in your identity provider
- The client ID, client secret, and issuer URL from your IdP

## Quick Setup (Environment Variables)

<Aside type="note">
SSO is an enterprise feature. Set `NEOBOARD_EDITION=enterprise` in your environment to enable it.
</Aside>

The fastest way to enable SSO. Set these variables and restart NeoBoard:

```bash
NEOBOARD_EDITION=enterprise
OIDC_ISSUER=https://myorg.okta.com
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=neoboard
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
```

That's it — an SSO button will appear on the login page.

### All Environment Variables

| Variable | Required | Default | Description |
|----------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `OIDC_ISSUER` | Yes | — | OIDC issuer URL (e.g., `https://myorg.okta.com`) |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | Yes | — | OIDC client identifier |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | Yes | — | OIDC client secret |
| `OIDC_DISPLAY_NAME` | No | `SSO` | Button label on the login page |
| `OIDC_SCOPES` | No | `openid profile email` | OIDC scopes to request |
| `OIDC_CLAIM_KEY` | No | — | IdP claim key for role mapping (e.g., `groups`) |
| `OIDC_ADMIN_VALUE` | No | — | Claim value(s) that map to Admin role (comma-separated) |
| `OIDC_CREATOR_VALUE` | No | — | Claim value(s) that map to Creator role (comma-separated) |
| `OIDC_READER_VALUE` | No | — | Claim value(s) that map to Reader role (comma-separated) |
| `OIDC_AUTO_PROVISION` | No | `true` | Auto-create users on first SSO login |
| `OIDC_DEFAULT_ROLE` | No | `creator` | Role when no claim matches |
| `OIDC_ENFORCE_SSO` | No | `false` | Hide password form for non-admin users |

### Docker Compose Example

```yaml
services:
  neoboard:
    image: neoboard:latest
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://neoboard:neoboard@db:5432/neoboard
      ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${ENCRYPTION_KEY}
      NEXTAUTH_SECRET: ${NEXTAUTH_SECRET}
      NEXTAUTH_URL: https://neoboard.example.com
      # Enterprise + SSO
      NEOBOARD_EDITION: enterprise
      OIDC_ISSUER: https://myorg.okta.com
      OIDC_CLIENT_ID: neoboard-prod
      OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET: ${OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET}
      OIDC_DISPLAY_NAME: Company SSO
      OIDC_CLAIM_KEY: groups
      OIDC_ADMIN_VALUE: devops,platform-team
      OIDC_CREATOR_VALUE: engineering,data-team
      OIDC_READER_VALUE: marketing,sales
```

## Multi-Provider Setup (Admin UI)

<Aside type="note">
For multiple SSO providers, use the Admin UI in Settings > Authentication. The env-based provider and UI-based providers work together.
</Aside>

For organizations that need multiple SSO providers (e.g., Okta + Azure AD), use the Admin UI. The env-based provider and UI-based providers work together — the env provider appears first on the login page.

### Configuring a Provider

<Steps>

1. **Log in as an admin** and navigate to **Settings > Authentication**

2. **Click "Add Provider"** and fill in the form:

   | Field | Description | Example |
   |-------|-------------|---------|
   | Display Name | Shown on the login button | `Company SSO` |
   | Issuer URL | Your IdP's OIDC issuer endpoint | `https://login.example.com/realms/myorg` |
   | Client ID | The OIDC client identifier | `neoboard-prod` |
   | Client Secret | The OIDC client secret (stored encrypted) | `abc123...` |
   | Scopes | OIDC scopes to request | `openid profile email` (default) |

3. **Configure role mapping** (optional) to map IdP group claims to NeoBoard roles:

   | Field | Description | Example |
   |-------|-------------|---------|
   | IdP Claim Key | The token claim containing groups | `groups` or `realm_access.roles` |
   | Admin | Claim value that maps to Admin role | `neoboard-admins` |
   | Creator | Claim value that maps to Creator role | `neoboard-editors` |
   | Reader | Claim value that maps to Reader role | `neoboard-viewers` |

4. **Set provisioning options:**

   - **Auto-provision new users** — When enabled, users signing in via SSO for the first time are automatically created in NeoBoard. When disabled, only pre-existing users can use SSO.
   - **Default role** — The role assigned when no claim mapping matches (default: Creator).
   - **Enforce SSO** — When enabled, the password login form is hidden for non-admin users. Admins can still use password login via `?password=true` in the URL.

5. **Click "Add Provider"** to save

</Steps>

The SSO button will appear on the login page immediately.

## IdP Configuration Examples

### Okta

<Steps>

1. In the Okta admin console, go to **Applications > Create App Integration**
2. Select **OIDC - OpenID Connect** and **Web Application**
3. Set the redirect URI to: `https://your-neoboard-domain/api/auth/callback/sso-{provider-id}`
4. Note the **Client ID** and **Client Secret**
5. The issuer URL is your Okta domain: `https://your-org.okta.com`
6. To map groups: go to **Directory > Groups**, create groups like `neoboard-admins`, assign users
7. In the app's **Sign On** settings, add a **Groups claim** with filter `Matches regex: neoboard-.*`

</Steps>

In NeoBoard Settings > Authentication:
```
Display Name:    Okta
Issuer URL:      https://your-org.okta.com
Client ID:       0oa1234567890abcdef
Client Secret:   your-client-secret
Claim Key:       groups
Admin value:     neoboard-admins
Creator value:   neoboard-editors
Reader value:    neoboard-viewers
```

### Azure AD / Entra ID

<Steps>

1. In the Azure portal, go to **App Registrations > New Registration**
2. Set the redirect URI to: `https://your-neoboard-domain/api/auth/callback/sso-{provider-id}`
3. Under **Certificates & Secrets**, create a new client secret
4. Under **Token Configuration**, add the `groups` optional claim to the ID token
5. The issuer URL is: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/v2.0`

</Steps>

In NeoBoard Settings > Authentication:
```
Display Name:    Azure AD
Issuer URL:      https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/v2.0
Client ID:       your-app-client-id
Client Secret:   your-client-secret
Claim Key:       groups
Admin value:     {group-object-id-for-admins}
Creator value:   {group-object-id-for-editors}
```

<Aside type="tip">
Azure AD returns group object IDs (GUIDs) in the `groups` claim, not group names. Use the group's Object ID from the Azure portal as the mapping value.
</Aside>

### Keycloak

<Steps>

1. In the Keycloak admin console, create a new **Client** in your realm
2. Set **Client authentication** to On (confidential client)
3. Set the redirect URI to: `https://your-neoboard-domain/api/auth/callback/sso-{provider-id}`
4. Under **Client Scopes > neoboard-dedicated**, add a **Group Membership** mapper with claim name `groups`
5. Create groups (e.g., `neoboard-admins`, `neoboard-editors`) and assign users

</Steps>

In NeoBoard Settings > Authentication:
```
Display Name:    Keycloak
Issuer URL:      https://keycloak.example.com/realms/your-realm
Client ID:       neoboard
Client Secret:   your-client-secret
Claim Key:       groups
Admin value:     neoboard-admins
Creator value:   neoboard-editors
Reader value:    neoboard-viewers
```

### Google Workspace

<Steps>

1. In the Google Cloud Console, go to **APIs & Services > Credentials**
2. Create an **OAuth 2.0 Client ID** (Web application)
3. Set the redirect URI to: `https://your-neoboard-domain/api/auth/callback/sso-{provider-id}`
4. The issuer URL is: `https://accounts.google.com`

</Steps>

<Aside type="caution">
Google's OIDC tokens don't include a `groups` claim by default. All Google SSO users will get the **default role** unless you use Google Workspace directory groups with a custom claim mapper.
</Aside>

## Role Mapping

Role mapping is evaluated on **every login**, not just the first time. If a user's group membership changes in the IdP, their NeoBoard role updates automatically on their next sign-in.

**Priority order:** Admin > Creator > Reader. If a user is in multiple mapped groups, the highest-priority role wins.

**Multiple groups per role:** Use comma-separated values to map several IdP groups to the same NeoBoard role:

```bash
OIDC_ADMIN_VALUE=devops,platform-team,it-ops
OIDC_CREATOR_VALUE=engineering,data-team,analytics
OIDC_READER_VALUE=marketing,sales,support
```

If a user belongs to any of the listed groups, they get that role. This also works in the Admin UI claim mapping fields.

**Nested claims** are supported with dot notation. For example, Keycloak's `realm_access.roles` claim can be mapped with:

```
Claim Key: realm_access.roles
```

When no claim mapping is configured, or no claim matches, the **default role** is used.

## Account Linking

When an SSO user's email matches an existing password-based NeoBoard account, the accounts are automatically linked. The user can then sign in with either method. The SSO login will update the user's role based on the latest IdP claims.

## Limits

- Up to **5 SSO providers** can be configured per tenant
- Client secrets are encrypted at rest using AES-256-GCM (same encryption as database connection credentials)
- Provider configurations are cached for 60 seconds — changes take up to 1 minute to propagate

## Deleting a Provider

When you delete an SSO provider:

- Users who were provisioned via that provider **keep their accounts**
- They can no longer sign in via SSO for that provider
- If they have a password set, they can still use password login
- An admin can assign them a new password in **Users** management

## Troubleshooting

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| "Invalid parameter: redirect_uri" | The redirect URI in your IdP doesn't match. Set it to `https://your-domain/api/auth/callback/sso-{provider-id}` where `{provider-id}` is the provider's ID in NeoBoard (visible in Settings > Authentication URL). |
| SSO button not showing | Check that the provider is **Enabled** in Settings > Authentication. The public endpoint only returns enabled providers. |
| User gets wrong role | Verify the claim key and values match exactly what your IdP sends. Check the IdP's token debugger to inspect the actual claims. |
| "Auto-provision is disabled" error | The user doesn't exist in NeoBoard and auto-provisioning is turned off. Create the user manually first, or enable auto-provisioning. |
| Login loops back to /login | Ensure `NEXTAUTH_URL` is set correctly in your environment and matches the URL users access NeoBoard from. |
Use API keys to access NeoBoard programmatically.

API keys let you access NeoBoard's REST API without a browser session. They are useful for scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and integrations.

## Creating an API Key

1. Navigate to **Settings > API Keys** in the sidebar
2. Click **Create API Key**
3. Enter a **name** (e.g., "CI Pipeline") and optional **expiration date**
4. Click **Create**
5. **Copy the key immediately** -- it is shown only once and cannot be retrieved later

The key starts with `nb_` followed by a random string.

## Using an API Key

Include the key in the `Authorization` header:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer nb_your_key_here" \
  https://your-neoboard.example.com/api/dashboards
```

**JavaScript / fetch:**

```javascript
const response = await fetch("https://your-neoboard.example.com/api/dashboards", {
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer nb_your_key_here",
  },
});
const data = await response.json();
```

**Python / requests:**

```python
import requests

response = requests.get(
    "https://your-neoboard.example.com/api/dashboards",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer nb_your_key_here"},
)
data = response.json()
```

## Available Endpoints

All data endpoints support API key authentication (38 of 45 total endpoints). The only exceptions are:

| Endpoint | Reason |
|----------|--------|
| `/api/auth/*` | Session-only (NextAuth handlers) |
| `/api/auth/bootstrap-status` | Public (no auth required) |
| `/api/docs` | Public (documentation page) |
| `/api/openapi`, `/api/openapi.json` | Public (API specification) |

### Common Operations

| Operation | Method | Endpoint |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| List dashboards | `GET` | `/api/dashboards` |
| Get dashboard | `GET` | `/api/dashboards/:id` |
| Create dashboard | `POST` | `/api/dashboards` |
| Export dashboard | `GET` | `/api/dashboards/:id/export` |
| Import dashboard | `POST` | `/api/dashboards/import` |
| Execute query | `POST` | `/api/query` |
| Execute write query | `POST` | `/api/query/write` |
| List connections | `GET` | `/api/connections` |
| Test connection | `POST` | `/api/connections/:id/test` |
| Fetch schema | `GET` | `/api/connections/:id/schema` |
| List users (admin) | `GET` | `/api/users` |
| Create user (admin) | `POST` | `/api/users` |

For the full API specification, visit `/api/docs` or `/api/openapi.json` on your NeoBoard instance.

## Key Management

| Operation | Method | Endpoint |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| List your API keys | `GET` | `/api/keys` |
| Create a new key | `POST` | `/api/keys` |
| Revoke a key | `DELETE` | `/api/keys/:id` |

### Expiration

Keys can have an optional expiration date. Expired keys return `401 Unauthorized`. The `lastUsedAt` field is updated on each use for audit purposes.

## Error Responses

Unauthenticated requests return:

```json
{ "error": "Unauthorized" }
```

With HTTP status `401`. Ensure your key is:
- Correctly prefixed with `nb_`
- Not expired
- Not revoked
- Included in the `Authorization` header (not query params)

## Security Notes

- API keys are hashed with HMAC-SHA256 before storage. NeoBoard never stores the plain-text key.
- Keys inherit the permissions of the user who created them (role, tenantId, canWrite).
- Revoked keys are immediately invalid.
- Use short expiration dates for temporary access.
Build a dashboard with your first widget in under 10 minutes.

This guide walks you through logging in, creating a dashboard, and adding your first chart widget.

## 1. Log In

Open NeoBoard in your browser. You will see the login screen.

![NeoBoard login screen](/screenshots/login.png)

Enter your email and password. If you are using the demo environment, the default credentials are:

- **Email**: `admin@neoboard.local`
- **Password**: `admin123`

Click **Sign In** to continue.

## 2. Create a New Dashboard

After logging in, you land on the dashboard list.

![Dashboard list](/screenshots/dashboard-list.png)

1. Click the **New Dashboard** button in the top-right corner.
2. Enter a **name** for your dashboard (e.g., "Movie Analytics").
3. Add an optional **description** to help others understand its purpose.
4. Click **Create**.

You are now in **edit mode** on your new, empty dashboard.

## 3. Add Your First Widget

1. Click the **Add Widget** button in the toolbar.
2. In the widget editor dialog, select a **connection** from the dropdown. This tells NeoBoard which database to query. If you have not added a connection yet, see the [Connecting to Your Database](/connections/connecting-databases) guide first.
3. Choose a **chart type**. For your first widget, **Bar Chart** is a great choice. It works well with most data shapes.

## 4. Write a Query

Type a query into the query editor. Here are two examples depending on your database.

**Neo4j (Cypher):**

```cypher
MATCH (m:Movie)
RETURN m.title AS label, m.released AS value
ORDER BY m.released DESC
LIMIT 10
```

**PostgreSQL (SQL):**

```sql
SELECT name, email
FROM "user"
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10
```

> The SQL example above queries the built-in `user` table. Replace it with your own table if you have loaded custom data.

Your query should return at least two columns. The chart will use the first column as labels and the second as values.

## 5. Preview and Save

1. Click **Run** to preview the results. You will see your data rendered as a bar chart below the query editor.
2. If the chart looks good, click **Save** to add the widget to your dashboard.
3. You can **drag** the widget to reposition it or **resize** it by dragging its edges.

## 6. Exit Edit Mode

Click the **Edit** toggle in the toolbar to exit edit mode. Your dashboard is now live. Anyone with access can view it.

## Next Steps

- Add more widgets to build a complete dashboard.
- Explore all available [widget types](/dashboards/widgets) including tables, graphs, maps, and forms.
- Set up database connections in [Connecting to Your Database](/connections/connecting-databases).
- Control who can see your dashboards in [Managing Users and Permissions](/administration/managing-users).

Widgets are the building blocks of dashboards. Each widget runs a query and displays the result as a chart, table, graph, or form.

## Widget Types

| Type | What it shows | Expected data |
|------|--------------|---------------|
| Bar Chart | Vertical or horizontal bars | Rows with a category column and a value column |
| Line Chart | Time series and trend lines | Rows with an x-axis column and one or more y-axis columns |
| Pie Chart | Proportional slices | Rows with a label column and a value column |
| Single Value | One large number (KPI) | A single row with one column |
| Table | Sortable, paginated data grid | Any tabular result |
| Graph | Nodes and relationships (Neo4j) | Graph data (nodes and edges) |
| Map | Geographic markers on a map | Rows with latitude and longitude columns |
| JSON Viewer | Collapsible JSON tree | Any query result |
| Form | Input fields that run a write query | User-defined form fields |

## How to Create a Widget

The widget editor walks you through five steps:

1. **Connection** — pick which database to query
2. **Query** — write a Cypher or SQL query
3. **Chart type** — choose how to visualize the result
4. **Options** — map columns, set colors, configure axes and labels
5. **Save** — the widget appears on your dashboard

Click **Run** at any point to preview the result before saving.

## Parameter Widgets

Parameter widgets collect user input and pass it to other widgets' queries. They do not display data themselves.

| Parameter type | Input control | Value produced |
|---------------|---------------|----------------|
| Select | Dropdown (populated by a seed query) | Single string |
| Text | Free-text input | String |
| Number | Numeric input | Number |
| Date | Date picker | ISO date string |
| Date Range | Start/end date pickers | `{start, end}` object |
| Boolean | Toggle switch | `true` or `false` |
| Multiselect | Multi-value dropdown | Array of strings |
| Slider | Range slider | Number |

Other widgets reference parameter values with `$param_name` in their queries. See [Parameters](/dashboards/parameters) for details.

## Widget Templates (Widget Lab)

You can save any widget configuration as a reusable template in the Widget Lab.

Interactive filters that drive queries across widgets.

Parameters make dashboards interactive. A user picks a value from a dropdown, types into a text field, or selects a date — and every widget that references that parameter re-runs its query automatically.

## How It Works

1. You add a **parameter widget** to your dashboard (e.g., a dropdown)
2. The user selects a value
3. Other widgets reference the parameter with `$param_name` in their queries
4. When the value changes, dependent widgets refresh automatically

## The `$param_name` Syntax

Use `$param_name` anywhere in your query to reference a parameter value. NeoBoard replaces it safely using parameterized queries — values are never interpolated into the query string.

**Cypher (Neo4j):**

```cypher
MATCH (m:Movie)
WHERE m.year >= $param_start_year
  AND m.year <= $param_end_year
RETURN m.title, m.year
ORDER BY m.year
```

**SQL (PostgreSQL):**

```sql
SELECT title, year
FROM movies
WHERE year >= $param_start_year
  AND year <= $param_end_year
ORDER BY year;
```

The parameter name must match exactly. If your parameter widget is named `start_year`, reference it as `$param_start_year` (NeoBoard adds the `param_` prefix automatically).

## Parameter Types

| Type | Input control | Value produced | Use case |
|------|--------------|----------------|----------|
| Select | Dropdown | Single string | Filter by category (e.g., country, status) |
| Text | Free-text input | String | Search by name or keyword |
| Number | Numeric input | Number | Filter by threshold or ID |
| Date | Date picker | ISO date string | Filter by specific date |
| Date Range | Start/end pickers | `{start, end}` | Filter a time window |
| Boolean | Toggle switch | `true` / `false` | Enable/disable a filter |
| Multiselect | Multi-value dropdown | Array of strings | Filter by multiple categories |
| Slider | Range slider | Number | Adjust a numeric threshold visually |

## Seed Queries

For **Select** and **Multiselect** parameters, you write a seed query that populates the dropdown options. The seed query runs once when the dashboard loads.

**Example seed query (Cypher):**

```cypher
MATCH (c:Country)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS value
ORDER BY c.name
```

**Example seed query (SQL):**

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT country AS value
FROM customers
ORDER BY country;
```

The query must return a column named `value`. Each row becomes a dropdown option.

## Where Parameter Values Come From

- **User input** — the user selects or types a value (default)
- **Seed query** — a query populates dropdown options
- **Default values** — initial values set during widget configuration
- **Click actions** — clicking a chart element sets a parameter value (configured in the widget's Advanced tab)

2. Click **Add Connection**.

4. Fill in the connection details:

|-------|---------|-------|

| **URI** | `bolt://localhost:7687` | Bolt protocol URI |
| **Username** | `neo4j` | Your Neo4j username |

## Adding a PostgreSQL Connection

1. Navigate to **Connections** in the sidebar.
2. Click **Add Connection**.
3. Select **PostgreSQL** as the connection type.
4. Fill in the connection details:

| Field | Example | Notes |
|-------|---------|-------|
| **Name** | Analytics DB | A label to identify this connection |
| **URI** | `postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb` | Full connection string |

## Troubleshooting

If you see an **Error** badge next to your connection, try these steps.

### Check Your URI and Credentials

Make sure the URI, username, and password are correct. A typo in any field will cause a connection failure.

### Docker Networking

If NeoBoard and your database both run in Docker, use the **container name** instead of `localhost`:

```

postgresql://user:pass@neoboard-postgres:5432/mydb
```

If your database runs directly on your machine (not in Docker), use `localhost` with the correct port:

- Neo4j Bolt: `7687` (default)
- PostgreSQL: `5432` (default)

Ensure no firewall rules block traffic between NeoBoard and your database. Cloud-hosted databases may require you to allowlist the NeoBoard server IP.

How NeoBoard connects to Neo4j and PostgreSQL databases.

Connectors are the bridge between NeoBoard and your databases. Each connector stores encrypted credentials and manages a connection pool.

![Connections management page](/screenshots/connections.png)

## Supported Databases

| Database | Protocol | Query Language |
|----------|----------|---------------|
| Neo4j | `bolt://`, `neo4j://` | Cypher |
| PostgreSQL | `postgresql://` | SQL |

## Setting Up a Connection

1. Go to **Connections** in the sidebar
2. Click **Add Connection**
3. Fill in the form fields:

| Field | Description | Example |
|-------|-------------|---------|
| Name | A label you will see in dropdowns | `Movie Database` |
| Type | Neo4j or PostgreSQL | `Neo4j` |
| URI | Database connection string | `bolt://localhost:7687` |
| Username | Database user | `neo4j` |
| Password | Database password | `password` |

4. Click **Test Connection** to verify connectivity
5. Click **Save**

## Connection Lifecycle

1. **Create** — you provide URI, username, and password
2. **Encrypt** — credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before storage
3. **Test** — NeoBoard verifies connectivity before saving
4. **Pool** — a connection pool is created on first query
5. **Cache** — the pool is reused for subsequent queries to the same database

## Credential Security

- Credentials are encrypted at rest using AES-256-GCM (envelope encryption with HKDF-SHA256)
- Plaintext credentials are never logged or stored
- If `ENCRYPTION_KEY` is lost, all stored credentials become unrecoverable

## Advanced Settings

| Setting | Description | Default |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| Connection Timeout | Time to establish a connection | 30s |
| Query Timeout | Maximum query execution time | 30s |
| Max Pool Size | Maximum concurrent connections | 10 |
| Idle Timeout | Time before idle connections close | 10s |
| Statement Timeout | PostgreSQL statement timeout | (query timeout) |
| SSL Reject Unauthorized | Verify SSL certificates | true |

## Schema Introspection

NeoBoard can read your database schema to help with query writing:

- **Neo4j** — node labels, relationship types, property keys
- **PostgreSQL** — tables, columns, data types
How NeoBoard protects your databases from harmful queries.

NeoBoard enforces multiple layers of safety to protect your databases.

## Parameterized Queries

User input is **never** interpolated into query strings. All parameters use the database driver's native parameterization:

- **Neo4j**: Cypher parameters (`$param_name`)
- **PostgreSQL**: Positional parameters (`$1`, `$2`)

## Read-Only by Default

Non-form widgets execute queries in read-only mode:

- **PostgreSQL**: `BEGIN READ ONLY` transactions
- **Neo4j**: Read access mode sessions

Write operations are only allowed through **Form widgets** with the `can_write` permission, enforced server-side.

## Timeouts

Every query has a timeout enforced at the driver level:

- Default: 30 seconds (configurable via `QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS`)
- Uses `AbortSignal` for PostgreSQL
- Native timeout for Neo4j driver

## Row Limits

Results are consumed with a `MAX_ROWS + 1` pattern:
- The extra row detects if results were truncated
- NeoBoard **never** adds `LIMIT` clauses to user queries
- Default limit: 1000 rows

## Concurrency Control

Each connector uses a per-connection queue (`p-queue`) to prevent overwhelming the database with concurrent queries.

## Credential Protection

- AES-256-GCM encryption at rest
- HKDF-SHA256 key derivation per credential
- Decrypted credentials never logged
- Lost `ENCRYPTION_KEY` = unrecoverable credentials
Create users, assign roles, and control access in NeoBoard.

NeoBoard uses role-based access control to manage what each user can see and do. This guide covers user creation, roles, and the write permission toggle.

![Users management page](/screenshots/users.png)

## Roles

Every user is assigned one of three roles.

| Role | Dashboards | Connections | Users | Write Queries |
|------|-----------|-------------|-------|---------------|
| **Admin** | View, create, edit, delete | Manage all connections | Create and manage users | Yes (if enabled) |
| **Creator** | View, create, edit, delete own | View connections | No access | Yes (if enabled) |
| **Reader** | View only | No access | No access | No |

- **Admin** has full access to everything: dashboards, connections, user management, and settings.
- **Creator** can build and edit dashboards and widgets. Creators can run queries against connections but cannot add or modify connections.
- **Reader** can only view published dashboards. Readers cannot edit anything or run custom queries.

## Write Permission

The **write permission** toggle is an additional control, separate from the role. It determines whether a user can execute write queries (e.g., `CREATE`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`).

- When **enabled**, the user can run queries that modify data.
- When **disabled**, the user is restricted to read-only queries, regardless of their role.

This is useful when you want a Creator to build dashboards but not modify the underlying data.

## Creating a User

1. Navigate to **Users** in the sidebar.
2. Click **Create User**.
3. Fill in the user details:
   - **Name**: The user's display name
   - **Email**: Their login email address
   - **Password**: A strong initial password
   - **Role**: Select Admin, Creator, or Reader
4. Toggle **Write permission** on or off based on your needs.
5. Click **Create**.

The new user can now log in with their email and password.

## API Keys

For programmatic access to NeoBoard, you can generate API keys.

![Settings page](/screenshots/settings.png)

1. Navigate to **Settings** in the sidebar.
2. Go to the **API Keys** section.
3. Click **Create API Key**.
4. Copy the key immediately. It will not be shown again.

Use the API key in the `Authorization` header when calling the NeoBoard REST API.

Tenant isolation and data security in NeoBoard.

NeoBoard supports multi-tenancy for SaaS deployments and team isolation.

## How It Works

- Every table in the metadata database has a `tenant_id` column
- Every database query includes a tenant filter at the ORM level
- JWT tokens include a `tenantId` claim, validated before any data access

## Isolation Guarantees

- Users in tenant A **cannot** see or modify data belonging to tenant B
- Connections, dashboards, widgets, and API keys are all tenant-scoped
- Admin users have full access within their tenant only

## Roles

| Role | Permissions |
|------|------------|
| **Admin** | Full access to all resources in the tenant |
| **Creator** | Create/edit own dashboards, view connections |
| **Reader** | View-only access to shared dashboards |

## Configuration

Multi-tenancy is controlled by environment variables — no code branches:

- `DEFAULT_TENANT_ID`: Used for single-tenant deployments
- Tenant assignment happens at user creation time

Email and password authentication in NeoBoard.

NeoBoard ships with built-in email/password authentication. No external identity provider is required.

## First Admin Setup

When NeoBoard starts for the first time with an empty database, the first user to sign up becomes the **Admin**. This bootstrap flow:

1. Navigate to `/signup`
2. If `ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` is set in your environment, enter it in the bootstrap token field
3. Fill in your name, email, and password
4. Click **Create account**

You are now the first Admin and can create additional users.

## Signing In

1. Navigate to `/login`
2. Enter your email and password
3. Click **Sign in**

If SSO is configured, SSO buttons appear above the password form. Both login methods work simultaneously unless SSO enforcement is enabled.

## Password Requirements

- Minimum 8 characters
- At least 1 letter
- At least 1 number

## Forced Password Change

Admins can require a user to change their password on next login by enabling **Force password change** when creating or editing a user. The user will be redirected to `/change-password` before they can access any dashboard.

## Session Management

- Sessions use JWT tokens (stateless)
- Default session duration: 8 hours (configurable via `SESSION_MAX_AGE`)
- Sessions are invalidated when:
  - A user's password is changed (with a 30-second grace period)
  - A user is disabled by an admin
  - A user's role is changed

## Rate Limiting

Login attempts are rate-limited by IP address:

- **20 login attempts** per minute per IP
- **10 signup attempts** per minute per IP

Exceeding the limit silently rejects further attempts until the window resets.

## Registration Control

Set `REGISTRATION_ENABLED=false` to disable the `/signup` page. Existing users can still log in, and admins can still create users via the Users management page.

Understand NeoBoard's role-based access control system.

Every NeoBoard user is assigned one of three roles. Roles determine what a user can see and do across the application.

## Role Comparison

| Capability | Admin | Creator | Reader |
|-----------|-------|---------|--------|
| View dashboards | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Create/edit dashboards | Yes | Yes (own) | No |
| Delete dashboards | Yes | Yes (own) | No |
| Manage connections | Yes | View only | No |
| Manage users | Yes | No | No |
| Access settings | Yes | No | No |
| Run read queries | Yes | Yes | No |
| Run write queries | Yes (if enabled) | Yes (if enabled) | No |

## Admin

Full access to everything: dashboards, connections, user management, and settings. Admins are the only role that can create other users and configure SSO providers.

## Creator

Can build and edit their own dashboards and widgets. Creators can run queries against existing connections but cannot add, modify, or delete connections. They cannot access user management or settings.

## Reader

View-only access. Readers can view dashboards shared with them but cannot edit anything, run custom queries, or access connections.

## Write Permission

The **write permission** toggle is an additional control, independent of the role. It determines whether a user can execute write queries (`CREATE`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`).

| Role | Write Permission On | Write Permission Off |
|------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Admin | Can write | Can write (always) |
| Creator | Can write | Read-only queries |
| Reader | No effect | No effect |

Admins always have write access regardless of the toggle. This is useful when you want a Creator to build dashboards but not modify the underlying data.

## Role Assignment

### At user creation
Admins assign a role when creating a user in **Users** management.

### Via SSO claim mapping
When SSO is configured, roles can be automatically assigned based on IdP group claims. See [SSO Role Mapping](/authentication/sso#role-mapping).

### Default role
New SSO users who don't match any claim mapping get the configured **default role** (defaults to Creator).
